decks.title: Plant Growth and Development — Part 1: Germination, growth and differentiation
goals: Distinguish hypogeal, epigeal and viviparous germination with two examples each
Describe the phases of growth, the sigmoid curve and how an auxanometer measures growth
Distinguish differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation with examples

slides.heading: From seed to plant
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a seed germinates, how growth is measured, and how cells become specialised.

visual.alt: Seed to germination to growth to differentiation to mature plant

slides.narration: A plant begins as a seed. It germinates, grows by cell division and enlargement, and its cells then specialise. Plants keep growing throughout life, because meristems stay active.

slides.heading: Three kinds of germination
slides.body_md: The difference lies in **which part of the seedling elongates** and what happens to the **cotyledons**. In **viviparous** germination the seed germinates **inside the fruit on the parent plant**.

slides.heading: Growth in a root tip: zones and phases
slides.body_md: Growth in a meristem has **three phases**: **cell division** (meristematic), **elongation** (cells enlarge by taking in water and forming a vacuole) and **maturation** (differentiation). They are seen in order up a root tip.

slides.narration: At the very tip is the root cap. Above it, cells divide. Higher up, the new cells take in water and become long. Higher still, they mature into specialised cells, and root hairs form.

slides.heading: Arithmetic and geometric growth
slides.body_md: In **arithmetic growth** only one daughter cell keeps dividing, so length rises by a constant amount: $L_t = L_0 + rt$. In **geometric growth** both daughters divide, so size rises faster and faster: $W_t = W_0 e^{rt}$.

rows: Root or shoot elongating at a steady rate
Early growth of a seedling or a culture of cells

visual.alt: Table comparing arithmetic and geometric growth

slides.narration: In arithmetic growth the root lengthens by the same amount each day. In geometric growth the number of cells doubles again and again, so growth speeds up as the organism gets larger.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: arithmetic and geometric growth
slides.body_md: A root is 3 cm long and grows at 0.8 cm a day. A single cell divides every 12 hours, and both daughters keep dividing. Find the root length after 5 and 10 days, and the number of cells after 72 hours.
bullets: Doublings in 72 hours $= 72 \div 12 = 6$.

visual.alt: Worked table: arithmetic and geometric growth

slides.narration: The root gains a fixed amount each day, so its length is a straight line. The cells double six times in three days, which gives sixty-four cells from one.

slides.heading: The sigmoid growth curve
slides.body_md: Growth of a plant organ or a whole plant plotted against time gives an **S-shaped (sigmoid) curve** with a **lag phase**, a **log (exponential) phase** of fastest growth and a **stationary phase** as growth slows.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: absolute and relative growth rate
slides.body_md: Seedling A grows from 10 cm to 16 cm and seedling B from 30 cm to 36 cm, each in 3 days. Compare their absolute and relative growth rates.
bullets: Absolute rate: A $= \dfrac{6}{3} = 2$ cm a day; B $= 2$ cm a day.
Relative rate $=$ growth $\div$ initial size $\div$ time: A $= \dfrac{6}{10 \times 3} = 0.2$, or 20 percent a day.
B $= \dfrac{6}{30 \times 3} \approx 0.0667$, or about 6.7 percent a day.

visual.alt: Worked table: equal absolute rates, relative rates 20 and 6.7 percent

slides.narration: Both seedlings gain the same length each day, so their absolute rates are equal. But the first was smaller to start with, so it has grown much more in proportion to its size. Its relative growth rate is three times higher.

slides.heading: Quick check: relative growth rate
slides.body_md: Calculate a relative growth rate.
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide the growth by the starting size and by the time.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading the auxanometer
slides.body_md: The pointer of an arc auxanometer is 24 cm long and the pulley radius is 2 cm. The pointer moves 18 mm in a day. Find the actual growth of the shoot, and the pointer movement for a growth of 3 mm.
bullets: Magnification $= 24 \div 2 = 12$.
Growth $= 18 \div 12 = 1.5$ mm.
Pointer movement for 3 mm of growth $= 3 \times 12 = 36$ mm.

visual.alt: Worked table: 1.5 mm of growth

slides.narration: The pointer is twelve times longer than the pulley is wide, so it magnifies growth twelve times. To find the real growth, divide the pointer movement by twelve.

slides.heading: Measuring growth and the factors that affect it
slides.body_md: Growth can be measured **directly** (by a scale, or by counting leaves) and in many other ways. Several **external factors** control it.

rows: Length with a scale or thread; leaf area; number of leaves
Fresh weight, dry weight, volume, cell number

visual.alt: Table of ways of measuring growth and factors affecting it

slides.narration: Growth can be followed by length, number of leaves, area, fresh weight or dry weight. Plants need water for cell enlargement, oxygen for respiration, nutrients to build new material, a suitable temperature and light.

slides.heading: Differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation
slides.body_md: Cells made by **meristems** become specialised, and some can regain the power to divide.

rows: Meristematic cells become specialised in structure and function
Cells become xylem vessels, with lignified walls and loss of protoplasm
Mature cells regain the power to divide
Interfascicular cambium and cork cambium form from permanent cells; callus in tissue culture
Dedifferentiated cells lose the power to divide again and mature
Secondary xylem and cork formed from the cambia

visual.alt: Table of differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation with examples

slides.narration: Differentiation makes specialised cells. Dedifferentiation is when specialised cells begin to divide again, as in the formation of cork cambium. Redifferentiation is when the new cells mature and specialise once more.

slides.heading: Quick check: differentiation
slides.body_md: Name the process in which a mature cell regains the power to divide.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of cork cambium forming in an old stem.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Germination: epigeal (hypocotyl elongates), hypogeal (epicotyl elongates), viviparous (mangrove, on the plant).
Phases of growth: division, elongation, maturation; arithmetic and geometric growth; sigmoid curve with lag, log and stationary phases.
Growth rates: absolute (2 cm a day for both seedlings) and relative (20 against 6.7 percent a day); auxanometer magnifies growth 12 times.
Differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation; plants keep open growth and plasticity.

visual.alt: Summary table of germination types

slides.narration: To recap: seeds germinate in three ways. Growth has division, elongation and maturation phases and follows an S-shaped curve. An auxanometer magnifies growth. Cells differentiate, and may dedifferentiate and redifferentiate.

bullets: Name **the part that elongates** and give **two examples** for each type of germination.
Draw the **sigmoid curve** with three labelled phases and axes.
Show **working** for growth rates and auxanometer readings, with units.
Define the **three differentiation terms** with an example each.

decks.title: Plant Growth and Development — Part 2: Plant growth regulators and their uses
goals: Describe how auxin was discovered (Went’s experiments)
State four physiological effects of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and abscisic acid
Suggest a growth regulator for uses such as rooting cuttings, ripening fruit or weed control

slides.heading: Chemical messengers of plants
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the five groups of plant growth regulators, how auxin was found, and how they are used in farming and gardening.

visual.alt: The five groups of plant growth regulators

slides.narration: Plant growth regulators are small chemicals made in tiny amounts that control growth. Auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins mostly promote growth, while abscisic acid inhibits it. Ethylene is a gas with several roles.

slides.narration: Went collected the growth substance from coleoptile tips in agar blocks. When he placed a block off centre on a headless coleoptile, the coleoptile bent. The substance, named auxin, speeds up elongation on the side where it is.

slides.heading: Steps in the discovery of the growth regulators
slides.body_md: Each regulator was found through an experiment or an observation.

rows: Darwin (1880): coleoptile tip senses light; Boysen-Jensen: a chemical passes through gelatin; Went (1928): isolated in agar
Kurosawa: rice seedlings with bakanae (foolish seedling) disease, caused by the fungus Gibberella
Skoog and Miller (1955): kinetin from old DNA promoted cell division in tissue culture
Cousins: gas from ripe oranges ripened bananas
Isolated as a growth inhibitor from dormant buds and abscising organs

visual.alt: Table of the discovery of the five plant growth regulators

slides.narration: Darwin showed that the tip detects light. Went isolated auxin in agar. Kurosawa traced the foolish seedling disease of rice to a fungal chemical, now called gibberellin. Skoog and Miller found kinetin, and Cousins found that ripe oranges give off ethylene.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the Avena curvature test
slides.body_md: In a curvature test, an agar block with 0.4 mg of auxin per litre gave a curvature of 12 degrees, and curvature is proportional to concentration in this range. Find the curvature for 0.8 mg per litre, and the concentration that gives 21 degrees.
bullets: Curvature per mg per litre $= 12 \div 0.4 = 30$ degrees.
At 0.8 mg per litre: $30 \times 0.8 = 24$ degrees.
For 21 degrees: $21 \div 30 = 0.7$ mg per litre.

x.label: Auxin in the agar block (mg per litre)

visual.alt: Angle of curvature of the coleoptile rising in a straight line with the auxin concentration of the agar block

slides.narration: Because curvature is proportional to concentration, find the angle for one unit and scale up or down. Twice the auxin gives twice the bending. This made the coleoptile a way to measure auxin.

slides.heading: Quick check: curvature test
slides.body_md: Work out an unknown concentration from the curvature.
slides.narration: Quick check. Curvature is proportional to concentration.

slides.heading: Auxins: four effects
slides.body_md: **Auxins** (IAA, IBA, NAA, 2,4-D) are made in shoot tips and root tips and move **down the plant**.

rows: The shoot tip stops the growth of lateral buds; removing the tip releases them
Cause fruits to form without fertilisation (seedless tomato)
Stop early fall of young leaves and fruits
Cell elongation; 2,4-D is a weedicide for broadleaf weeds

visual.alt: Table of effects of auxins

slides.narration: Auxins make cells in stems elongate. They keep side buds dormant, which is apical dominance. They make cuttings root, can produce seedless fruit, and delay the falling of young fruits and leaves.

slides.heading: Gibberellins and cytokinins: four effects each
slides.body_md: Gibberellins mainly affect **elongation and dormancy**; cytokinins mainly affect **cell division and ageing**.

rows: Increase the length of stems (bolting; sugarcane)
Break seed and bud dormancy; make barley seeds produce amylase in malting
Promote growth of lateral buds, overcoming apical dominance
Increase the size and stalk length of fruits such as grapes; parthenocarpy
Delay leaf senescence by keeping chlorophyll and protein
Promote bolting and flowering in some plants
Help shoot formation in tissue culture

visual.alt: Table of four effects each of gibberellins and cytokinins

slides.narration: Gibberellins lengthen stems, break dormancy and enlarge fruits. Cytokinins make cells divide, wake lateral buds, delay the yellowing of leaves and help shoots form in tissue culture.

slides.heading: Ethylene and abscisic acid: four effects each
slides.body_md: **Ethylene** is a **gas**; **abscisic acid (ABA)** is the **stress hormone** and growth inhibitor.

rows: Promotes abscission of leaves and fruits and senescence
Maintains seed dormancy and inhibits germination
Promotes flowering in pineapple and mango, and female flowers in cucumber
Breaks seed and bud dormancy; promotes root hairs

visual.alt: Table of four effects each of ethylene and abscisic acid

slides.narration: Ethylene ripens fruit, loosens leaves and fruits so that they fall, and promotes flowering in some plants. Abscisic acid closes the stomata in a drought, keeps seeds dormant, and slows growth.

slides.heading: Quick check: ethylene and abscisic acid
slides.body_md: Match an effect to its regulator.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which regulator closes stomata?

slides.heading: Regulators working together
slides.body_md: The **ratio of auxin to cytokinin** controls development. In tissue culture a high auxin to cytokinin ratio gives **roots**, a low ratio gives **shoots**, and a balance gives **callus**. In the plant, **auxin from the shoot tip** and **cytokinin from the roots** pull in opposite directions on lateral buds.

visual.alt: Table of auxin and cytokinin levels in three culture media

slides.narration: No regulator acts alone. A rich auxin medium makes roots, a rich cytokinin medium makes shoots, and equal amounts keep the tissue as a lump called callus. Apical dominance is a balance between auxin and cytokinin.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: predicting the organ
slides.body_md: Three media have these auxin and cytokinin amounts (mg/L): M1 2 and 0.2; M2 0.2 and 2; M3 1 and 1. Predict what a callus forms on each.
bullets: **M2**: ratio 0.2 ÷ 2 = 0.1, so **shoots**.
**M3**: ratio 1 ÷ 1 = 1, so **undifferentiated callus**.

visual.alt: Worked table of ratios and predicted organs

slides.narration: Divide auxin by cytokinin. A ratio far above one favours roots, far below one favours shoots, and a ratio of one leaves the callus undifferentiated.

slides.heading: Choosing a growth regulator
slides.body_md: Match the **job** to the **regulator**.

rows: Seedless and larger grapes; longer sugarcane stems; malting barley
Keeping cut flowers and vegetables fresh

visual.alt: Table of agricultural and horticultural uses of growth regulators

slides.narration: Auxin roots cuttings and stops fruit fall, and the strong auxin 2,4-D kills broadleaf weeds. Ethylene ripens fruit. Gibberellins make seedless grapes and longer sugarcane. Cytokinins keep cut flowers fresh.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: preparing a spray
slides.body_md: A farmer needs 2000 mL of a 50 ppm (mg per litre) spray of a regulator from a 1000 ppm stock. How much stock and water, and how many mg of regulator are in the spray?
bullets: Regulator $= 50 \times 2 = 100$ mg.

visual.alt: Worked table: dilution of a regulator stock

slides.narration: Use the dilution rule: stock volume equals the wanted strength times the wanted volume, divided by the stock strength. Here one tenth of a litre of stock is made up to two litres with water.

slides.heading: Quick check: uses
slides.body_md: Choose a regulator for a given use.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which regulator would a fruit trader use?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Went (1928) isolated auxin from oat coleoptile tips in agar; curvature is proportional to auxin.
Auxins: apical dominance, rooting, parthenocarpy, prevent abscission. Gibberellins: stem elongation, dormancy breaking, larger fruit, bolting.
Cytokinins: cell division, lateral buds, delay senescence, shoot formation. Ethylene: ripening, abscission, flowering. ABA: stomatal closure, dormancy, inhibition.
Uses: rooting (auxin), ripening (ethylene), weed control (2,4-D), seedless grapes (gibberellin), freshness (cytokinin).

visual.alt: Summary table of one key effect of each regulator

slides.narration: To recap: Went showed that a chemical from the tip, auxin, bends coleoptiles. Each of the five regulators has four main effects, and each has an agricultural or horticultural use.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Describe **Went’s experiment** with agar blocks, the off-centre placement and the curvature.
Give **four effects** for each regulator, using the key words.
Name the **regulator** for each use: rooting, ripening, weeds, seedless fruit.
Keep **promoters** (auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin) apart from **inhibitors** (ABA).
slides.narration: Exam tips. Describe Went’s experiment step by step. Give four effects of each regulator. Name the right regulator for each farming use. And keep the promoters apart from the inhibitor, abscisic acid.

notes.title: Plant Growth and Development — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Seed germination: hypogeal, epigeal and viviparous
sections.body_md:
**Germination** is the growth of the embryo of a seed into a seedling when it gets water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. The radicle comes out first and forms the root system, and the plumule forms the shoot. The way the cotyledons behave gives three types.

- **Epigeal germination** — the **hypocotyl** elongates and pushes the **cotyledons above the soil**, where they may turn green and photosynthesise for a while. Examples: **castor, bean, cotton, sunflower, cucumber, tamarind**.
- **Hypogeal germination** — the **epicotyl** elongates, and the **cotyledons stay below the soil**, supplying food. Examples: **pea, gram, maize, mango** (and other cereal grains).
- **Viviparous germination** — the seed **germinates inside the fruit while it is still attached to the parent plant**. The radicle grows out of the fruit and the heavy seedling drops into the mud and takes root quickly. It is characteristic of **mangroves**, which grow in marshy, salty soil. Examples: **Rhizophora, Sonneratia** (also Heritiera in some books).

| Feature | Epigeal | Hypogeal | Viviparous |
|---|---|---|---|
| Part that elongates | hypocotyl | epicotyl | radicle, inside the fruit |
| Cotyledons | above soil | in soil | inside fruit on the plant |
| Examples | castor, bean | pea, maize | Rhizophora, Sonneratia |

key_terms.definition_md: Cotyledons raised above the soil by an elongating hypocotyl.
Cotyledons stay in the soil; the epicotyl elongates.
Seed germinates within the fruit on the parent plant, as in mangroves.

sections.heading: 2. Phases of growth, growth rate, measurement and factors
sections.body_md:
**Growth** is a permanent, irreversible increase in size, usually with an increase in dry weight. Plant growth is **open**: meristems keep dividing throughout life, at root tips, shoot tips (**primary growth**) and cambia (**secondary growth**).

**Phases of growth in a meristem** (seen in order up a root tip): **meristematic phase** (cells divide, small, dense cytoplasm, thin walls); **elongation phase** (cells take in water, form a large vacuole and enlarge, and walls are laid down); **maturation phase** (cells reach final size and differentiate).

**Growth rate:** the increase in growth per unit time. In **arithmetic growth**, only one daughter cell keeps dividing: L(t) = L₀ + rt, a straight line (for example a root with L₀ = 3 cm and r = 0.8 cm a day is 11 cm after 10 days). In **geometric growth**, both daughters divide: W(t) = W₀e^(rt); in cells that double every 12 hours one cell gives 64 cells in 72 hours. **Absolute growth rate** is the total growth per unit time; **relative growth rate** is the growth per unit time **as a proportion of the initial size** (two seedlings both growing 2 cm a day, one from 10 cm and one from 30 cm, have relative rates 20 and 6.7 percent a day).

**Sigmoid curve:** in a model shoot growing to 60 cm, there is a **lag phase** (slow, to about day 4), a **log or exponential phase** (fastest; about 7.5 cm a day at day 10; to about day 16) and a **stationary phase** when growth slows as nutrients, water and space become limiting.

**Measuring growth:** directly, by length with a scale or thread, number of leaves, leaf area, volume, fresh weight, dry weight and cell number. The **auxanometer** is an indirect method for the growth of a shoot: in the **arc auxanometer** a thread from the shoot tip passes over a pulley of radius r carrying a pointer of length R over an arc scale, so the pointer exaggerates the growth by R ÷ r (here 24 ÷ 2 = 12 times); actual growth = pointer movement ÷ 12.

**Factors affecting growth:** water (cell enlargement), oxygen (respiration), nutrients (building materials), temperature and light.

sections.heading: 3. Differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation
sections.body_md:
**Differentiation:** cells derived from meristems mature to perform specific functions, with changes in structure. Example: a cell becomes a **xylem vessel**, losing its protoplasm and depositing **lignin** in its walls. **Dedifferentiation:** differentiated, mature cells **regain the capacity to divide**. Examples: the **interfascicular cambium** forms from parenchyma between vascular bundles; the **cork cambium** forms from cortical cells; **callus** forms from tissue in culture. **Redifferentiation:** the cells produced by a dedifferentiated tissue **lose the capacity to divide again and mature** to perform specific functions. Examples: **secondary xylem and phloem** formed from the vascular cambium; **cork** formed from the cork cambium.

**Sequence of developmental processes:** a seed germinates and grows by **cell division → cell enlargement → differentiation → maturation** of tissues and organs, then flowering, fruiting and **senescence**. Development is the sum of growth and differentiation. Plants show **plasticity**: the form depends on the environment or the stage of life, as in **heterophylly** (different leaf shapes on one plant, for example cotton, coriander and larkspur, or different shapes in air and water in buttercup).

sections.heading: 4. Plant growth regulators
sections.body_md:
**Plant growth regulators (PGRs)** are small, simple chemicals, made in tiny amounts, that control growth and development. **Promoters:** auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins. **Inhibitor:** abscisic acid. **Ethylene** is a gas with promoting and inhibiting roles.

**Discovery of auxin:** **Charles and Francis Darwin (1880)** found that the tip of a canary-grass coleoptile detects light and that an influence passes down to the bending region. **Boysen-Jensen** showed that the influence passes through a block of gelatin but not through mica. **F. W. Went (1928)** cut off the tips of oat (*Avena*) coleoptiles, placed them on **agar blocks** and placed the blocks **off-centre** on decapitated coleoptiles; the coleoptiles **curved away from the block** because the cells on the block side elongated more. The chemical was named **auxin**. In the **Avena curvature test**, the angle of curvature is proportional to the auxin concentration in the block (illustrative: 30 degrees for each mg per litre).

**Gibberellins:** found from the rice *bakanae* ("foolish seedling") disease caused by the fungus *Gibberella fujikuroi* (Kurosawa). **Cytokinins:** kinetin was found by **Skoog and Miller (1955)** in old or autoclaved DNA; zeatin from maize. **Ethylene:** ripening of fruit near ripe oranges (Cousins). **ABA:** isolated as a growth inhibitor.

| Regulator | Four effects |
|---|---|
| **Auxins** (IAA, IBA, NAA, 2,4-D) | **apical dominance**; **rooting** of cuttings; **parthenocarpy**; prevent **abscission** of young leaves and fruits (also cell elongation; 2,4-D kills broadleaf weeds) |
| **Gibberellins** (GA₃) | **elongation** of stems (bolting; sugarcane); **break dormancy** of seeds and buds (barley malting); increase **fruit size** (grapes) and parthenocarpy; promote **bolting and flowering** |
| **Cytokinins** (kinetin, zeatin) | promote **cell division**; promote **lateral bud growth**; **delay senescence** of leaves; **shoot formation** in tissue culture |
| **Ethylene** | **ripening** of fruits; promotes **abscission** and senescence; promotes **flowering** in pineapple and mango and **female flowers** in cucumber; breaks dormancy and promotes root hairs |
| **Abscisic acid** | **closes stomata** under water stress; maintains **seed dormancy**; **inhibits growth**; promotes leaf **senescence** and abscission |

**Interaction:** the auxin to cytokinin ratio controls organ formation in culture: M1 (2 : 0.2, ratio 10) gives roots; M2 (0.2 : 2, ratio 0.1) gives shoots; M3 (1 : 1, ratio 1) gives undifferentiated callus.

sections.heading: 5. Agricultural and horticultural applications
sections.body_md:
- **Rooting of cuttings:** auxins such as **IBA and NAA**.
- **Ripening of fruits and synchronised flowering:** **ethylene**, supplied as **ethephon**, which releases ethylene; ethylene or NAA brings pineapple to flower together.
- **Weed control:** **2,4-D**, a synthetic auxin, kills broadleaf (dicot) weeds in cereal fields without harming the narrow-leaved crop.
- **Preventing premature fruit and leaf drop:** auxins (NAA) in orchards.
- **Seedless fruits and larger fruits:** **gibberellins** on grapes; auxins for seedless tomato.
- **Increasing sugar yield:** gibberellins lengthen sugarcane stems, so more sugar is made. **Malting:** gibberellins make barley seeds form amylase.
- **Keeping cut flowers and vegetables fresh, delaying senescence:** **cytokinins**.
- **Tissue culture:** auxin and cytokinin in the right ratio; **cucumber:** ethylene for more female flowers.
- **Spray preparation:** a spray is made by diluting a stock using C₁V₁ = C₂V₂; for example 2000 mL of 50 ppm from a 1000 ppm stock needs 100 mL of stock.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up hypocotyl and epicotyl: the hypocotyl lifts the cotyledons in epigeal germination; the epicotyl grows in hypogeal germination.
- Calling viviparous germination a type that happens in soil (it happens on the parent plant, in mangroves).
- Giving absolute growth rate when relative growth rate is asked (divide by the initial size as well).
- Dividing by the pointer length instead of multiplying by pulley radius over pointer length (growth = pointer movement ÷ magnification).
- Saying the coleoptile bends towards the agar block (it bends away from the block side in Went's experiment).
- Calling gibberellins or ethylene inhibitors; the inhibitor of the five is abscisic acid.
- Confusing dedifferentiation with redifferentiation.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: the part that elongates, an example of a type of germination, a regulator for a use, an assertion-reason on apical dominance or stomata.
- 2–3-mark questions: types of germination compared; phases of growth; sigmoid curve; differentiation terms; Went's experiment; four effects of a regulator.
- 5-mark questions in parts: sigmoid curve with phases and rate; auxanometer diagram and calculation; Went's experiment with effects of auxin; uses of regulators.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In epigeal germination the cotyledons appear above the ground.

**Reason (R):** In epigeal germination the cotyledons are usually green and make some food.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the colour of the cotyledons does not explain why they appear above ground; the hypocotyl lifts them — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: A mangrove seedling establishes itself quickly in marshy mud.

answer.model_answer_md: Its seed germinates on the parent plant, so the heavy seedling with a long radicle drops into the mud and fixes itself at once.

questions.solution_md: Vivipary.

marking_scheme.step: Viviparous germination; seedling drops and roots

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between epigeal and hypogeal germination, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: In **epigeal** germination the **hypocotyl elongates** and raises the **cotyledons above the soil**, as in **castor** or bean. In **hypogeal** germination the **epicotyl elongates** and the **cotyledons stay in the soil**, as in **pea** or maize.

questions.solution_md: Two types.

questions.stem_md: What is viviparous germination? Name two plants in which it occurs and the habitat in which they live.

answer.model_answer_md: **Viviparous germination** is the germination of the seed **inside the fruit while it is still attached to the parent plant**. It occurs in **mangroves** such as **Rhizophora** and **Sonneratia**, which live in **marshy, saline** coastal soil.

questions.solution_md: Definition, plants, habitat.

questions.stem_md: Compare epigeal, hypogeal and viviparous germination in terms of the part that elongates and the position of the cotyledons, with one example each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Epigeal:** the **hypocotyl** elongates and the **cotyledons are lifted above the soil** (castor, bean). **Hypogeal:** the **epicotyl** elongates and the **cotyledons remain in the soil** (pea, maize). **Viviparous:** the seed **germinates inside the fruit on the parent plant**, the **radicle** grows out of the fruit, and the seedling then falls into the mud (Rhizophora).

questions.solution_md: Three types.

options.text_md: a large central vacuole and thick lignified walls
no nucleus and a wide lumen
dense cytoplasm, thin walls and a large nucleus

questions.solution_md: Meristematic cells are small, thin-walled, with dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In geometric growth the rate of increase keeps rising because

options.text_md: both daughter cells formed at each division keep dividing
only one daughter cell keeps dividing
the cells divide only in the dark
the dividing cells all differentiate at once

questions.solution_md: When both daughter cells divide, the number of cells rises exponentially — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Name the three phases of growth seen in a root tip, from the tip upwards, and state one feature of each.

answer.model_answer_md: The **meristematic phase**, where cells are small and **divide**; the **elongation phase**, where cells **absorb water, form a vacuole and enlarge**; and the **maturation phase**, where cells reach their final size and **differentiate** into specialised tissues.

questions.stem_md: How does an arc auxanometer measure the growth of a shoot?

answer.model_answer_md: A **thread** from the shoot tip passes over a small **pulley** and carries a **weight**. As the shoot grows, the pulley turns and a long **pointer** fixed to it moves over an **arc scale**. Because the pointer is much longer than the pulley radius, growth is **magnified**; **actual growth = pointer movement × pulley radius ÷ pointer length**.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between absolute growth rate and relative growth rate.

answer.model_answer_md: **Absolute growth rate** is the **total growth per unit time**, for example centimetres per day. **Relative growth rate** is the growth per unit time **expressed as a proportion of the initial size**, so it allows two organs of different size to be compared fairly.

questions.stem_md: Describe the sigmoid growth curve of a plant, naming its three phases and the reason for the last one.

answer.model_answer_md: The curve is S-shaped. In the **lag phase** growth is **slow** as the cells prepare to divide. In the **log (exponential) phase** growth is **fastest**, because the cells divide and enlarge rapidly. In the **stationary phase** growth **slows and stops**, because **nutrients, water and space become limiting** and the organ reaches maturity.

questions.stem_md: Name three external factors that affect plant growth and state the role of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Water** is needed for cell enlargement, since cells grow by taking in water. **Oxygen** is needed for respiration, which supplies energy for growth. **Nutrients** supply the raw materials for new protoplasm and cell walls. (**Temperature** controls the rate of enzyme reactions, and **light** affects the form of the plant.)

questions.solution_md: Three factors.

questions.stem_md: Seedling X grows from 10 cm to 16 cm and seedling Y from 30 cm to 36 cm over the same 3 days. Calculate the absolute and relative growth rate of each, and say which is growing faster in relation to its size.

answer.model_answer_md: **Absolute rate:** X = (16 − 10) ÷ 3 = **2 cm a day**; Y = **2 cm a day**, the same. **Relative rate:** X = 6 ÷ 10 ÷ 3 = **20 percent a day**; Y = 6 ÷ 30 ÷ 3 = about **6.7 percent a day**. So **seedling X** is growing faster in relation to its size.

questions.stem_md: State the sequence of developmental processes by which a germinated seed becomes a mature plant body.

answer.model_answer_md: After germination the plant grows by **cell division** in meristems, then **cell enlargement**, followed by **differentiation** of cells into tissues and **maturation** of organs. Development includes **growth and differentiation**, and later flowering, fruiting and **senescence**.

questions.stem_md: Define redifferentiation and give one example from the plant body.

answer.model_answer_md: **Redifferentiation** is the process in which cells produced by a **dedifferentiated** tissue **lose the capacity to divide again** and **mature** to perform specific functions. For example, the cells formed by the **cork cambium** mature into **cork**, and those from the vascular cambium into secondary xylem.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation, with one example each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Differentiation:** cells made by meristems mature into specialised structure and function, such as a **xylem vessel** with lignified walls. **Dedifferentiation:** mature cells **regain the power to divide**, such as the **interfascicular cambium** or **cork cambium**, or callus in culture. **Redifferentiation:** the cells formed by such a tissue **mature and lose the power to divide**, such as **secondary xylem** or **cork**.

(b) Give one example of each in a woody stem. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Differentiation** is the maturation of cells from meristems into specialised cells. **Dedifferentiation** is the regaining of the power to divide by mature cells. **Redifferentiation** is the loss of that power and maturation of the cells formed by dedifferentiated tissue.

questions.stem_md: State four physiological effects of auxins.

answer.model_answer_md: Auxins cause **apical dominance**, in which the shoot tip inhibits lateral buds; they promote **rooting** of stem cuttings; they cause **parthenocarpy**, the formation of seedless fruits; and they **prevent the early fall (abscission)** of young leaves and fruits.

questions.solution_md: Four effects.

questions.stem_md: State four physiological effects of gibberellins.

answer.model_answer_md: Gibberellins make **stems elongate** (bolting, longer sugarcane stems); they **break the dormancy** of seeds and buds (in barley they induce amylase for malting); they **increase fruit size** and cause parthenocarpy, as in grapes; and they promote **bolting and flowering**.

questions.solution_md: Four effects.

questions.stem_md: State four physiological effects of cytokinins.

answer.model_answer_md: Cytokinins promote **cell division**; they promote the growth of **lateral buds**, overcoming apical dominance; they **delay senescence** of leaves by keeping them green; and they promote **shoot formation** in tissue culture.

questions.solution_md: Four effects.

questions.stem_md: State four physiological effects of ethylene.

answer.model_answer_md: Ethylene **ripens fruits**; it promotes **abscission** of leaves and fruits and senescence; it promotes **flowering** in pineapple and mango and **female flowers** in cucumber; and it **breaks the dormancy** of seeds and buds and promotes root hairs.

questions.solution_md: Four effects.

questions.stem_md: State four physiological effects of abscisic acid.

answer.model_answer_md: Abscisic acid **closes stomata** under water stress; it maintains **seed dormancy** and inhibits germination; it **inhibits growth**, including stem elongation; and it promotes **leaf senescence and abscission**.

questions.solution_md: Four effects.

questions.stem_md: Describe Went’s experiments on oat coleoptiles that led to the discovery of auxin.

answer.model_answer_md: Went **cut off the tips** of oat (Avena) coleoptiles and placed them on **agar blocks** for some time, so that a growth substance diffused into the agar. He then placed these blocks **off-centre** on decapitated coleoptiles. The coleoptiles **curved away from the side with the block**, because the **cells on that side elongated more**. The substance was named **auxin**, and the angle of curvature depended on its concentration.

questions.stem_md: Classify the five plant growth regulators as promoters or inhibitors, giving one effect of each class.

answer.model_answer_md: The **promoters** are **auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins**; for example auxins make cells elongate and cause rooting, and cytokinins promote cell division. **Abscisic acid** is the **inhibitor**; it inhibits growth and maintains dormancy. **Ethylene** is a gaseous regulator with both roles: it promotes ripening and abscission, and it can inhibit elongation.

questions.solution_md: Classification.

marking_scheme.step: Ethylene as gas with both roles

questions.stem_md: A hedge is trimmed by cutting off the tips of its shoots. Explain, in terms of growth regulators, why it becomes bushy.

answer.model_answer_md: The **shoot tip makes auxin**, which moves down and **inhibits the growth of lateral buds**; this is **apical dominance**. Cutting off the tip **removes the source of auxin**, so the lateral buds are **released** and grow into branches. **Cytokinins**, which promote lateral bud growth, can then act, so the hedge becomes bushy.

questions.solution_md: Apical dominance.

questions.stem_md: A tissue culture worker has three media with auxin and cytokinin in mg per litre: M1 (2 and 0.2), M2 (0.2 and 2), M3 (1 and 1). Predict what a callus will form on each medium, with the reason.

answer.model_answer_md: The organ depends on the **auxin to cytokinin ratio**. **M1** has a ratio of 10, a high ratio, so the callus forms **roots**. **M2** has a ratio of 0.1, a low ratio, so it forms **shoots**. **M3** has equal amounts (ratio 1), so it stays as **undifferentiated callus**.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the experiment of F. W. Went that led to the discovery of auxin. [3]
(b) What conclusion did he draw? [1]
(c) State two other physiological effects of auxins. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Went **cut off the tips** of oat coleoptiles and placed them on **agar blocks** so that a chemical diffused into the agar. He placed the blocks **to one side** on the cut ends of **decapitated coleoptiles**. The coleoptiles **bent away from the block side**.

(b) A **chemical made in the coleoptile tip (auxin)** moves down and makes the cells on its side **elongate more**, and the amount of bending depends on its concentration.

(c) Auxins cause **apical dominance** and promote **rooting** of cuttings (or cause parthenocarpy).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the regulator discovered from the rice bakanae disease and the one named kinetin, and say how each was discovered. [2]
(b) State two physiological effects of each of these two regulators. [2]
(c) Which of the two delays the senescence of leaves? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Gibberellin** was discovered from the **bakanae (foolish seedling) disease of rice**, caused by the fungus **Gibberella** (Kurosawa). **Kinetin**, a **cytokinin**, was found by **Skoog and Miller** in **old or autoclaved DNA** as a substance that promoted cell division.

(b) **Gibberellin:** elongation of stems and breaking of seed dormancy. **Cytokinin:** promotes cell division and lateral bud growth.

(c) **Cytokinin**.

questions.solution_md: Ethephon releases ethylene, which ripens fruit — option (b).

questions.solution_md: 2,4-D, a synthetic auxin, kills dicot weeds in cereal fields — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A grower sprays grape vines with a regulator so that the bunches have larger, seedless berries. The regulator is
questions.solution_md: Gibberellins increase the size of grapes and cause parthenocarpy — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Apple growers spray their orchards with NAA before the fruit is ripe. The purpose is to

options.text_md: kill the weeds under the trees
prevent the early fall of fruits
make the fruits ripen at once

questions.solution_md: Auxins delay abscission and so reduce premature fruit drop — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A florist wants to keep cut leafy vegetables and flowers fresh for longer by delaying the yellowing of their leaves. Which regulator would help?
questions.solution_md: Cytokinins delay leaf senescence — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Spraying sugarcane plants with gibberellin increases the yield of sugar because it

options.text_md: lengthens the stems, which store the sugar
kills the weeds around the cane
makes the cane ripen and fall
stops the cane from flowering and dying

questions.solution_md: Gibberellins elongate the internodes, so more sugar is stored — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A grower needs 5 litres of a 20 ppm (mg per litre) spray of a regulator, from a stock of 1000 ppm. How many mL of stock are needed?
How many milligrams of regulator are present in 500 mL of a 100 ppm (mg per litre) solution?
Name two agricultural uses of ethylene and one of 2,4-D.

answer.model_answer_md: **Ethylene** (as ethephon) is used to **ripen fruits** such as banana and mango, and to **bring pineapple to flower together** (it also promotes female flowers in cucumber). **2,4-D**, a synthetic auxin, is used as a **weedicide** to kill **broadleaf (dicot) weeds** in cereal fields.

questions.stem_md: Name the growth regulator you would use, with a reason, for each of these: (i) ripening mature green bananas, (ii) producing larger seedless grapes, (iii) keeping cut flowers fresh.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Ethylene**, supplied as **ethephon**, because it **ripens fruit** and so brings the whole batch to ripeness together. (ii) **Gibberellin**, because it **increases fruit size** and causes **parthenocarpy**, so the grapes are larger and seedless. (iii) A **cytokinin**, because it **delays senescence** of the leaves and petals, keeping them fresh and green for longer.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the regulator suitable for (i) rooting of stem cuttings, (ii) killing broadleaf weeds, (iii) preventing fruit drop, (iv) breaking the dormancy of barley seeds in malting. [2]
(b) Calculate the volume of a 1000 ppm stock needed to prepare 2 litres of a 50 ppm spray and the volume of water to be added. [2]
(c) How many milligrams of regulator are in this spray? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) **Auxin (IBA, NAA)**; (ii) **2,4-D**; (iii) **auxin (NAA)**; (iv) **gibberellin**.

(b) **C₁V₁ = C₂V₂**: V₁ = 50 × 2000 ÷ 1000 = **100 mL** of stock, so water = 2000 − 100 = **1900 mL**.

(c) 50 mg per litre × 2 litres = **100 mg**.
